entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 10 1Co 10:1-33 . Danger of Fellowship with Idolatry Illustrated in the History of Israel: Such Fellowship Incompatible with Fellowship in the Lord's Supper. Even Lawful Things Are to Be Forborne, so as Not to Hurt Weak Brethren. 1. Moreover-- The oldest manuscripts read "for." Thus the connection with the foregoing chapter is expressed. Ye need to exercise self-denying watchfulness notwithstanding all your privileges, lest ye be castaways. For the Israelites with all their privileges were most of them castaways through want of it. ignorant-- with all your boasted "knowledge." our fathers-- The Jewish Church stands in the relation of parent to the Christian Church. all-- Arrange as the Greek, "Our fathers were all under the cloud"; giving the "all" its proper emphasis. Not so much as one of so great a multitude was detained by force or disease ( Psa 105:37 ) [Bengel]. Five times the "all" is repeated, in the enumeration of the five favors which God bestowed on Israel ( 1Co 10:1-4 ). Five times, correspondingly, they sinned ( 1Co 10:6-10 ). In contrast to the "all" stands "many (rather, 'the most') of them" ( 1Co 10:5 ). All of them had great privileges, yet most of them were castaways through lust. Beware you, having greater privileges, of sharing the same doom through a similar sin. Continuing the reasoning ( 1Co 9:24 ), "They which run in a race, run all, but one receiveth the prize." under the cloud-- were continually under the defense of the pillar of cloud, the symbol of the divine presence ( Ex 13:21 , 22 ; Psa 105:39 ; compare Is 4:5 ). passed through the sea-- by God's miraculous interposition for them ( Ex 14:29 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16940"/><div sID="gen33466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16940"/><hi type="bold">2. And--</hi>"And so" [Bengel].<div eID="gen33466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">baptized unto Moses--</hi>the servant of God and representative of the Old Testament covenant of the law: as Jesus, the Son of God, is of the Gospel covenant (<reference osisRef="John.1.17">Joh 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.3.5">He 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.6">6</reference>). The people were led to believe in Moses as God's servant by the miracle of the cloud protecting them, and by their being conducted under him safely through the Red Sea; therefore they are said to be "baptized unto" him (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.31">Ex 14:31</reference>). "Baptized" is here equivalent to "initiated": it is used in accommodation to Paul's argument to the Corinthians; they, it is true, have been "baptized," but so also virtually were the Israelites of old; if the virtual baptism of the latter availed not to save them from the doom of lust, neither will the actual baptism of the former save them. There is a resemblance between the symbols also: for the cloud and sea consist of water, and as these took the Israelites out of sight, and then restored them again to view, so the water does to the baptized [Bengel]. Olshausen understands "the cloud" and "the sea" as symbolizing the Spirit and water respectively (<reference osisRef="John.3.5">Joh 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.44-Acts.10.47">Ac 10:44-47</reference>). Christ is the pillar cloud that screens us from the heat of God's wrath. Christ as "the light of the world" is our "pillar of fire" to guide us in the darkness of the world. As the rock when smitten sent forth the waters, so Christ, having been once for all smitten, sends forth the waters of the Spirit. As the manna bruised in mills fed Israel, so Christ, when "it pleased the Lord to bruise Him," has become our spiritual food. A strong proof of inspiration is given in this fact, that the historical parts of Scripture, without the consciousness even of the authors, are covert prophecies of the future. <div eID="gen33467" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16941"/><div sID="gen33468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16941"/><hi type="bold">3. same spiritual meat--</hi>As the Israelites had the water from the rock, which answered to baptism, so they had the manna which corresponded to the other of the two Christian sacraments, the Lord's Supper. Paul plainly implies the importance which was attached to these two sacraments by all Christians in those days: "an inspired protest against those who lower their dignity, or deny their necessity" [Alford]. Still he guards against the other extreme of thinking the mere external possession of such privileges will ensure salvation. Moreover, had there been seven sacraments, as Rome teaches, Paul would have alluded to them, whereas he refers to only the two. He does not mean by "the same" that the Israelites and we Christians have the "same" sacrament; but that believing and unbelieving Israelites alike had "the same" spiritual privilege of the manna (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.17">1Co 10:17</reference>). It was "spiritual meat" or food; because given by the power of God's spirit, not by human labor [Grotius and Alford] <reference osisRef="Gal.4.29">Ga 4:29</reference>, "born after the Spirit," that is, supernaturally. <reference osisRef="Ps.78.24">Psa 78:24</reference>, "corn of heaven" (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.40">Psa 105:40</reference>). Rather, "spiritual" in its typical signification, Christ, the true Bread of heaven, being signified (<reference osisRef="John.6.32">Joh 6:32</reference>). Not that the Israelites clearly understood the signification; but believers among them would feel that in the type something more was meant; and their implicit and reverent, though indistinct, faith was counted to them for justification, of which the manna was a kind of sacramental seal. "They are not to be heard which feign that the old fathers did look only for transitory promises" [Article VII, Church of England], as appears from this passage (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2">He 4:2</reference>). <div eID="gen33468" type="x-p"/>

In <reference osisRef="Num.20.8">Nu 20:8</reference>, "the beasts" also are mentioned as having drunk. The literal water typified "spiritual drink," and is therefore so called.<div eID="gen33469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33470" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spiritual Rock that followed them--</hi>rather, "accompanied them." Not the literal rock (or its water) "followed" them, as Alford explains, as if Paul sanctioned the Jews' tradition (Rabbi Solomon on <reference osisRef="Num.20.2">Nu 20:2</reference>) that the rock itself, or at least the stream from it, followed the Israelites from place to place (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.9.21">De 9:21</reference>). But Christ, the "Spiritual Rock" (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.20">Psa 78:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">De 32:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.18">15, 18</reference>, 30, 31, 37; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.6">1Pe 2:6</reference>), accompanied them (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.15">Ex 33:15</reference>). "Followed" implies His attending on them to minister to them; thus, though mostly going before them, He, when occasion required it, followed "behind" (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.19">Ex 14:19</reference>). He satisfied all alike as to their bodily thirst whenever they needed it; as on three occasions is expressly recorded (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.24">Ex 15:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.17.6">17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.20.8">Nu 20:8</reference>); and this drink for the body symbolized the spiritual drink from the Spiritual Rock (compare <reference osisRef="John.4.13">Joh 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.14">14</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.3">1Co 10:3</reference>). <div eID="gen33470" type="x-p"/>

These are included in the "evil things," not that they are so in themselves, but they became so to the Israelites when they lusted after what God withheld, and were discontented with what God provided.

This all applied to the Corinthians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.1">1Co 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.9">6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.18">15, 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.10">1Co 8:10</reference>). If this were a real discrepancy, it would militate rather against inspiration of the subject matter and thought, than against verbal inspiration. The solution is: Moses in Numbers includes all who died "in the plague"; Paul, all who died "in one day"; one thousand more may have fallen the next day [Kitto, Biblical Cyclopædia]. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16947"/><div sID="gen33486" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16947"/><hi type="bold">9. tempt Christ--</hi>So the oldest versions, Irenæus (264), and good manuscripts read. Some of the oldest manuscripts read "Lord"; and one manuscript only "God." If "Lord" be read, it will mean Christ. As "Christ" was referred to in one of the five privileges of Israel (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.4">1Co 10:4</reference>), so it is natural that He should be mentioned here in one of the five corresponding sins of that people. In <reference osisRef="Num.21.5">Nu 21:5</reference> it is "spake against God" (whence probably arose the alteration in the one manuscript, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.9">1Co 10:9</reference>, "God," to harmonize it with <reference osisRef="Num.21.5">Nu 21:5</reference>). As either "Christ" or "Lord" is the genuine reading, "Christ" must be "God." Compare "Why do ye tempt the Lord?" (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.2">Ex 17:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.17.7">7</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.14.11">Ro 14:11</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.45.22">Is 45:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.23">23</reference>). Israel's discontented complainings were temptings of Christ especially, the "Angel" of the covenant (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.20">Ex 23:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.34">32:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Is 63:9</reference>). Though they drank of "that Rock ... Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.4">1Co 10:4</reference>), they yet complained for want of water (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.2">Ex 17:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.17.7">7</reference>). Though also eating the same spiritual meat (Christ, "the true manna," "the bread of life"), they yet murmured, "Our soul loatheth this light bread." In this case, being punished by the fiery serpents, they were saved by the brazen serpent, the emblem of Christ (compare <reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.26">He 11:26</reference>). The Greek for "tempt" means, tempt or try, so as to wear out the long-suffering of Christ (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.95.8">Psa 95:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.22">Nu 14:22</reference>). The Corinthians were in danger of provoking God's long-suffering by walking on the verge of idolatry, through overweening confidence in their knowledge. <div eID="gen33486" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16953"/><div sID="gen33500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16953"/>15. Appeal to their own powers of judgment to weigh the force of the argument that follows: namely, that as the partaking of the Lord's Supper involves a partaking of the Lord Himself, and the partaking of the Jewish sacrificial meats involved a partaking of the altar of God, and, as the heathens sacrifice to devils, to partake of an idol feast is to have fellowship with devils. We cannot divest ourselves of the responsibility of "judging" for ourselves. The weakness of private judgment is not an argument against its use, but its abuse. We should the more take pains in searching the infallible word, with every aid within our reach, and above all with humble prayer for the Spirit's teaching (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Ac 17:11</reference>). If Paul, an inspired apostle, not only permits, but urges, men to judge his sayings by Scripture, much more should the fallible ministers of the present visible Church do so.<div eID="gen33500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">To wise men--</hi>refers with a mixture of irony to the Corinthian boast of "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.10">1Co 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.19">2Co 11:19</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16957"/><div sID="gen33509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16957"/><hi type="bold">19-20. What say I then?--</hi>The inference might be drawn from the analogies of the Lord's Supper and Jewish sacrifices, that an idol is really what the heathen thought it to be, a god, and that in eating idol-meats they had fellowship with the god. This verse guards against such an inference: "What would I say then? that a thing sacrificed to an idol is any real thing (in the sense that the heathen regard it), or that an idol is any real thing?" (The oldest manuscripts read the words in this order. Supply "Nay") "But [I say] that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils (demons)." Paul here introduces a new fact. It is true that, as I said, an idol has no reality in the sense that the heathen regard it, but it has a reality in another sense; heathendom being under Satan's dominion as "prince of this world," he and his demons are in fact the powers worshipped by the heathen, whether they are or are not conscious of it (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.17">De 32:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.17.7">Le 17:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.15">2Ch 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.37">Psa 106:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.9.20">Re 9:20</reference>). "Devil" is in the Greek restricted to Satan; "demons" is the term applied to his subordinate evil spirits. Fear, rather than love, is the motive of heathen worship (compare the English word "panic," from Pan, whose human form with horns and cloven hoofs gave rise to the vulgar representations of Satan which prevail now); just as fear is the spirit of Satan and his demons (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.19">Jas 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen33509" type="x-p"/>

Conscience ... of the other--</hi>the weak brother introduced in <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.28">1Co 10:28</reference>.<div eID="gen33529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for why is my liberty judged off another man's conscience?--</hi>Paul passes to the first person, to teach his converts by putting himself as it were in their position. The Greek terms for "the other" and "another" are distinct. "The other" is the one with whom Paul's and his Corinthian converts' concern is; "another" is any other with whom he and they have no concern. If a guest know the meat to be idol meat while I know it not, I have "liberty" to eat without being condemned by his "conscience" [Grotius]. Thus the "for," &c., is an argument for <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.27">1Co 10:27</reference>, "Eat, asking no questions." Or, Why should I give occasion by the rash use of my liberty that another should condemn it [Estius], or that my liberty should cause the destruction of my weak brother?" [Menochius]. Or, the words are those of the Corinthian objector (perhaps used in their letter, and so quoted by Paul), "Why is my liberty judged by another's conscience?" Why should not I be judged only by my own, and have liberty to do whatever it sanctions? Paul replies in <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1Co 10:31</reference>, Your doing so ought always to be limited by regard to what most tends "to the glory of God" [Vatablus, Conybeare and Howson]. The first explanation is simplest; the "for," &c., in it refers to "not thine own" (that is, "not my own," in Paul's change to the first person); I am to abstain only in the case of liability to offend another's conscience; in cases where my own has no scruple, I am not bound, in God's judgment, by any other conscience than my own. <div eID="gen33530" type="x-p"/>
